titleStmt.title: An Exact Schedulability Analysis for Global Fixed-Priority Scheduling of the AER Task Model

analytic.title: An Exact Schedulability Analysis for Global Fixed-Priority Scheduling of the AER Task Model

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) multi-core platforms offer high performance and large availability of processing resources. Increased contention when accessing shared resources is a result of the high parallelism and one of the main challenges when realtime applications are deployed to these platforms. As a result, several execution models have been proposed to avoid contention by separating access to shared resources from execution.

In this work, we consider the Acquisition-Execution-Restitution (AER) model where contention to shared resources is avoided by design. We propose an exact schedulability test for the AER model under global fixed-priority scheduling using timed automata where we describe the schedulability problem as a reachability problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exact schedulability test for the AER model under global fixed-priority scheduling on multiprocessor platforms. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated using synthetic experiments and provides up to 65% more schedulable task sets than the state-of-the-art.

div.head: CCS CONCEPTS
div.p: • Computer systems organization → Real-time systems; Embedded software; • Software and its engineering → Real-time systems software.

Main memory access is a main source of contention. Thus, limiting the contention of memory access by design can increase the predictability of the system [17].

The Aquisition-Execution-Restitution (AER) model [6] has been proposed to achieve predictability of bus accesses to shared memory by avoiding simultaneous memory accesses. In this model, the task is divided into 3 phases, Aquisition (A), Execution (E), and Restitution (R) phase. All instructions and data required to perform the computations during the E-phase are read and copied to the local memory during the A-phase, allowing the task to perform the computations in the E-phase without having to access the main memory. After the E-phase is completed, the R-phase writes back the results to the main memory. Only one memory phase (Aquisition or Restitution) can run at the same time, avoiding contention on the shared memory access resource. Many researchers have proposed methods related to this model to achieve more predictable systems [14].

Schedulability analysis for the AER model under global fixedpriority scheduling has been proposed in [1] and [12]. These schedulability tests are only sufficient and therefore may classify a schedulable task set as unschedulable. In contrast, an exact schedulability test provides the result as unschedulable only when it is not actually schedulable. Therefore, having an exact schedulability test is needed to correctly evaluate the schedulability of a task set. Also, an exact test provides a reference to compare the accuracy of the existing schedulability tests. This work introduces an exact schedulability test for the AER model under global fixed-priority scheduling which we believe to be an important contribution to the real-time community.
The main contributions of the paper are:

• An exact schedulability test for the AER model under global fixed-priority scheduling. The schedulability test utilizes timed automata (TA) where the schedulability problem is described as a reachability problem. • Experimental results performed on synthetic task sets to evaluate the performance of the proposed test. Our test provides up to 65% more schedulable task sets than the state-of-theart, while providing acceptable solving times.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides details on related work. Section 3 provides an overview about our task model and the runtime execution model. Section 4 provides background details about the techniques used in this work. Section 5 explains the proposed exact schedulability analysis. Section 6 describes the experiments and presents the results obtained. Finally, Section 7 summarizes the findings of this work.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: Timing verification of multi-core real-time systems is a challenging topic and has received significant attention in recent years [11,14]. One approach to minimize contention to shared resources is to separate tasks into dedicated memory and execution phases, which improves the predictability of task execution on modern COTS platforms. The initial idea of the phased-execution model is presented by Pellizoni et al. [18] and is extended to the PRedictable Execution Model (PREM) [17]. In their paper, the periodic tasks are broken into two different types of intervals, predictable intervals and compatible intervals to increase predictability. The AER model falls under this category of phased-execution models and is a generalized version of the PREM model. The AER model is proposed by Durrieu et al. [6]. It separates memory operations and execution of a task by dividing it into three phases. Additionally, it removes contention when accessing the main memory by not allowing two memory phases at the same time. This model have been experimented with different priority assignment schemes using different properties of the tasks in [13]. A complete framework from high-level system specification to implementation on multi-core hardware has been proposed in [16] using the AER model. Scheduling algorithms have been proposed for this model using time-triggered scheduling [4] and partitioned scheduling [3]. In this work we focus on global scheduling which is also addressed by Maia et al. [12] and Alhammad et al. [1]. They proposed schedulability analysis for AER task model using global fixed-priority scheduling respectively using a memory perspective and a core perspective. Although these tests are efficient, they are not exact tests.

In this paper, we present an exact schedulability analysis for global fixed priority scheduling of the AER task model. We use TA in UPPAAL model checker for the test. TA and UPPAAL has been used by Guan et al. [8] and Yalcinkaya et al. [19] to propose exact schedulability analysis for other task models. In the analysis proposed in this paper we look at the task execution from the perspective of the shared memory resource where the task executes on the shared memory resource and suspends to perform computations on a processing core. A similar perspective has been used in [9] for their schedulability analysis.

div.head: SYSTEM OVERVIEW 3.1 Platform and Task Model
div.p: The multiprocessor system we consider has 𝑚 identical cores, where each core has a private, local memory (cache or scratchpad) with exclusive access. In this local memory, the instructions and data needed for the task that is running on the core can be stored and accessed when performing the computations. The shared memory can be accessed by all cores via a shared interconnect (for example a bus).

The task set is comprised of n independent tasks 𝜏 = {𝜏 1 , 𝜏 2 , ..., 𝜏 𝑛 }. Each task 𝜏 𝑖 can be represented by the tuple (𝑇 𝑖 , 𝐷 𝑖 , 𝑂 𝑖 , 𝑃 𝑖 , 𝐶 𝑖 ). Where, 𝑇 𝑖 , 𝐷 𝑖 , 𝑂 𝑖 and 𝑃 𝑖 represent the period, deadline, initial offset and the priority of the task respectively. The period and deadline are relative to the release time where, 𝐷 𝑖 ≤ 𝑇 𝑖 . A fixed priority value, 𝑃 𝑖 , is assigned to every task. Lower values of 𝑃 𝑖 denotes higher priority. 𝐶 𝑖 is the total execution time of the task. The utilization of a task can be represented as 𝑢 𝑖 = 𝐶 𝑖 /𝑇 𝑖 , where the total utilization of the task set is 𝑛 𝑖=1 𝑢 𝑖 . The tasks are divided into three phases, the Aquisition phase, Execute phase and Restitution phase 1 . All phases are executed in this sequence in a non-preemptive manner. In the A-phase the data and instructions needed to execute the task are copied from the main memory into the local memory of the core2 . Next is the execution phase, in which the computations are performed using the data and instructions that have been already stored in local memory. Thus the execution is performed without having to access the main memory and without any interference. Finally, the Rphase writes back the results at once to the main memory. The total execution time 𝐶 𝑖 is the addition of the times spent for the read phase (𝐶 where 𝑥 = {𝑟, 𝑒, 𝑤 }, depending whether it's the read, execute or write phase. The addition of the minimum timing values for each phase results in 𝐶 𝑚𝑖𝑛 𝑖 . Accordingly, the addition of the maximum timing values for each phase results in 𝐶 𝑚𝑎𝑥 𝑖 . Therefore, the total execution time can be represented by the tuple, ([

div.head: Runtime Execution Model
div.p: The tasks are scheduled according to global non-preemptive fixed priority scheduling. I.e. consecutive jobs of the same task can execute on different cores. The tasks are scheduled from a memory perspective. To avoid contention and to increase predictability, only one memory phase (read or write) is allowed to be scheduled at a time. Until the released tasks are scheduled, they are added to a global priority queue. Tasks are added to the priority queue before scheduling both their read and write phases. In this priority queue, the added tasks are sorted in ascending order of their priorities.

With the release of a task, it is added to the priority queue to schedule its read phase. For a read phase to be scheduled, the memory bus as well as one core must be available. A processing core is assigned to the task at the time its read phase is scheduled and this core is reserved for that task until its write phase completes. Thus, there can be only 𝑚 tasks active at the same time. However, the bus, which is a shared resource between all cores is released after each memory phase, allowing another memory phase to be scheduled. During the read phase, the memory bus is assigned to the task for the duration of 𝐶 𝑟 𝑖 , which allows for data transfer without contention. The completion of the read phase directly triggers the execution phase on the assigned core without the need for additional scheduling decisions. With the completion of the execution phase, the task is added to the same priority queue again until its write phase is scheduled. A write phase is scheduled if the memory bus is available. The bus is assigned to the task for the duration of 𝐶 𝑤 𝑖 , allowing to write back data to the main memory without contention. Once the write phase is completed, the task has completed its three phases and the corresponding processing core is freed and available to schedule another task.

Throughout the execution, the scheduler checks the priority queue. When the queue is not empty and the bus is available, it checks the following conditions according to task priority, starting with the task at the front of the queue.

C1 -If the task at the front wants its write phase to be scheduled, it is scheduled if the bus is available. C2 -If the task at the front wants its read phase to be scheduled, it will be scheduled if a core and the bus are available. C3 -If the task at the front wants its read phase to be scheduled and if a core is not available, the most prioritized write phase in the queue will proceed over the highest priority read phase at the front to free up a core for the read phase to be scheduled and to avoid a possible deadlock [4].

div.head: BACKGROUND
div.p: A timed automata is a finite automata model which is extended by introducing a finite set of real-valued clocks that are used to annotate the constraints and state transitions [2]. UPPAAL is a model checking tool that is built on the formal base of timed automata [5], which allows to model, simulate and verify real-time systems. Invariant and reachability properties are mainly checked by exploring the state space of the modeled networks of automata.

A query language is used to specify the properties that are intended to be checked. A location represents a state in the timed automata and is shown as a blue circle in UPPAAL models (see Figure 2). Location names are shown in maroon color. Progress conditions, called invariants added to a state/location are shown in pink text (Figure 2). Staying in a state is allowed only while these conditions are satisfied. A committed location is a special type of location in UPPAAL (Committed state in Figure 2(b)). Once entered into a committed state, it should be left immediately. Synchronization between different automata in the same UPPAAL model is achieved using channels which are represented in cyan color (refer to channels synch, first_synch and run in Figure 2). This is a handshake synchronization where, synch? proceeds when synch! is proceeded. Broadcast channels and urgent channels are two special types of channels in UPPAAL. An urgent channel must proceed without a delay when enabled and channel run in our model is defined as an urgent channel. A broadcast channel enables broadcast communication with any edge that has the same channel. In the model, synch and first_synch signals are defined as broadcast channels. Guard conditions are shown in green color where, they need to be satisfied for the corresponding edge transition to be enabled. Updates are shown in blue color. They are proceeded once the corresponding edge transitions are made.

div.head: Existing schedulability test using TA
div.p: Timed automata are used for schedulability tests [8,19]. The work of [19] presents a schedulability analysis for self-suspending tasks with fixed priorities, which are globally scheduled. Suspension of tasks can happen anytime during the execution. The upper part of Figure 1 depicts the self-suspension model (SSM), where the task suspends once during execution. The task executes as two sections, the execution section on a local processor and the suspension section on an accelerator.

Similarities can be observed between this self-suspension model and the AER model we consider (lower part of Figure 1). If readexecute-write phases of the AER model are viewed from the perspective of the memory access, the execution phase can be seen as equivalent to a suspension where the task is off-loaded to a processing core for the computational phase, and the read and write phases can be seen as equivalent to execution on the bus (see Figure 1). Therefore, from a memory perspective, the bus is equivalent to a single resource that executes memory phases, and the processing core is equivalent to a computational resource to which the suspended task is off-loaded. Considering the similarities between the 2 models, a task of the AER model can be represented by the SSM. Thus, a possible exact schedulability analysis can be obtained for the AER model.
However, while having these similarities, there are some differences between the two models that cannot be neglected. Therefore, applying the SSM to fit our AER model is non-trivial.

(1) Number of active task instances: In the self-suspension model, the amount of suspended tasks is not limited. In contrast, in the AER model, the number of tasks that can be off-loaded to processing cores for the execution phase from the bus (equivalent to suspension) is limited to the number of cores available on the platform. This needs to be accounted for when modelling the scheduler for the AER model. (2) Differentiate between read and write phases: Even though both read and write phases are equivalent to execution sections when applied to the SSM, there are non-trivial differences between the two memory phases. For a read phase to be started, a processing core must be available and allocated to the task. However, for the write phase, this condition does not have to be satisfied as a core has been already assigned before scheduling the read phase of the task. (3) Avoiding deadlocks: Consider a case where the task at the front of the priority queue is waiting for its read phase to be scheduled and all of the processing cores are occupied. In this case, the bus will be idle until a core is freed for the read phase at the front to be scheduled and will result in an under utilization of the shared memory access resource. Moreover, eventually if the most prioritized task of the task set is added to the priority queue to schedule its read phase, in this situation, the system will end up in a deadlock as it will wait forever for a core to be freed. As a solution, the most prioritized write phase in the priority queue needs to be scheduled over the read phase at the front.
Therefore, we propose a specific test for the AER model, which draws on concepts of the test proposed in [19], while the highlighted characteristics of our model are centrally considered.

div.head: SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: Our proposed schedulability analysis is a network of TA, which comprise of the TA of a task (Task), the scheduler (Sched) and the synchronizer (Sync), as shown in Figure 2. The Task automata model periodic, 3-phased, non-preemptive tasks of the AER model. The Sched automaton models the global scheduler of the system and the Sync automaton models the synchronizer, that synchronizes instances of Task automata. The system includes one Sched instance, one Sync instance and 𝑛 Task instances, one for each task.
In the model, an ID is assigned to each task to be used in between automata.

div.head: Task automaton
div.p: The Task automaton has six locations/states, Start, Queued, Memo-ryPhase, ExecutionPhase, Completed and Miss (refer to (a) of Figure 2). Two clocks, 𝑡 and 𝑥 are used in each Task automaton to keep track of the time. Clock 𝑡 keeps track of the release times and deadline misses of each task. Clock 𝑥 is used to keep track of the times spent in each state or each phase.

A task is kept in the Start state until it is released and in the case the task has an initial offset, it is forced to stay in Start until it passes its offset. When the task is released, it is moved to the Queued state. During this transition, the task is added to the priority queue and is specified as a task that is waiting to schedule its read phase. Thus, the scheduler knows that a processing core must be available to schedule it. When the task is in the Queued location, once the conditions for its read phase to be scheduled are satisfied, the task gets the run signal from the Sched automaton to be moved to the MemoryPhase location to start its read phase. During this transition, the task is removed from the priority queue and the number of available cores is decremented by one as a core is assigned to the task when its read phase is scheduled. The task stays in the MemoryPhase state for a minimum of 𝐶 𝑟 𝑚𝑖𝑛 𝑖 and a maximum of 𝐶 𝑟 𝑚𝑎𝑥 𝑖 period of time. The self-loops in the MemoryPhase and ExecutionPhase locations allow the task to stay in these states between the minimum and maximum times of the respective phase. The functions memory_min() and memory_max() returns the respective minimum and the maximum memory phase times of the current memory phase depending on if it is the read phase or the write phase. RT_min() and WT_min() in the UPPAAL model represents 𝐶 𝑟 𝑚𝑖𝑛 𝑖 and 𝐶 𝑤 𝑚𝑖𝑛 𝑖 respectively. Once the task has completed the read phase, it is moved to the ExecutionPhase state for its execution phase and the bus is freed during this transition. The task stays in the ExecutionPhase state for a time period between 𝐶 𝑒 𝑚𝑖𝑛 𝑖 and 𝐶 𝑒 𝑚𝑎𝑥 𝑖 , which are represented by ET_min() and ET_max() respectively in the UPPAAL model. Once the execution phase is completed, the task is moved to Queued once again until its write phase is scheduled. During this transition, the task is added to the priority queue and is specified as a task that is waiting to schedule its write phase. Similar to the read phase, the task is moved to the MemoryPhase state with the reception of run signal once the conditions are met for the write phase to be scheduled. It is kept in the MemoryPhase state for a time period in between 𝐶 𝑤 𝑚𝑖𝑛 𝑖 and 𝐶 𝑤 𝑚𝑎𝑥 𝑖 . Once the write phase is completed, the task is moved to the Completed state, during which, both the bus and the core that is allocated to the task are released. Once the task is moved to the Completed state, the task has completed the execution before its deadline for that particular instance of the task. As the task is periodic, it is released again once it reaches its period (t==period()). Clock 𝑡 is reset only at the beginning of a new period and its value is compared with the deadline at each state to check for deadline misses. In a case of a deadline miss, the task is moved to the Miss state.

Note: The (Task) automaton can be modified to model the execution of sporadic tasks in a similar way to [19]. The invariant condition of the Completed state should be removed and a self-loop can be added to the Completed state allowing the task to stay even after its period ends. Also, the guard condition when transitioning from Completed to Queued should be changed to t>=period(). However, we have not performed any experiments to test the scalability of our schedulability test for sporadic tasks.

div.head: Synch automaton
div.p: A system with un-synchronized task releases can result in schedules that contradict the assigned priorities [19]. Sync automaton's synch signal is broadcast to all instances of the Task automaton, synchronizing releases and transitions to make sure that all of the tasks with the same release time are released before the scheduler is triggered.

The Sync automaton has two locations, one committed location followed by the init location (see Figure 2(b)). This sends two signals back-to-back which covers the corner case where, a task completes the execution exactly on its deadline. It allows the task to reach the Queued state from MemoryPhase state, instantly after completing. The differentiation between synch and first_synch aligns Sync automaton's two signal sequence to the Task automaton's two-step transition to Queued state from the MemoryPhase state.

div.head: Sched automaton
div.p: The Sched automaton represents the scheduler of the system (Figure 2(c)). The run signal is defined as an urgent channel and is prioritized over the synch and first _synch signals as it should proceed without any delay.

As explained in Section 3.2, the scheduler checks the three conditions when the priority queue is not empty and the bus is available. Figure 2(c) depicts how these conditions correspond to the guard conditions of the Sched automaton. The function get_front() returns the task at the front of the priority queue. next_write() returns True if a write phase is found in the priority queue and satisfies this guard for that write phase to be scheduled. The function next_run() returns the next task to be scheduled. Once either of the three scheduling cases is satisfied, depending on the case, either the task at the front of the queue or the most prioritized task with a write phase in the queue is scheduled.

div.head: The reachability problem
div.p: We handle the schedulability test as a reachability problem, where, a task set is considered as schedulable if none of the tasks in the task set reaches the Miss state. The schedule and the schedulability of the task set depends on the time values each phase of each task takes. This results in a large number of possible scheduling scenarios. In order to exactly guarantee that the task set is schedulable under a certain configuration, the UPPAAL model checker checks the schedulability of all possible scheduling scenarios of the TA network.

div.head: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: This section presents the evaluation results of our exact test (ET) compared to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) [12] using randomly generated synthetic task sets. All of the experiments are performed on an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Silver 4114 CPU with 10 cores (20 threads) and 32GB of RAM, where the clock rate is 2.2GHz.

The common period values, {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 1000}𝑚𝑠 reported by Kramer et al. for automotive applications [10] are used with the associated probability percentages, {3, 2, 2, 25, 25, 3, 20, 1, 4} respectively to randomly generate period values. For a given total utilization 𝑈 , the Dirichlet-Rescale (DRS) algorithm [7] is used to randomly generate 𝑢 𝑖 utilization values for each task in the task is used to determine the time for the read and write phases where, 𝛾 is the fraction between the total time for the memory phases and the total execution time of the task. We consider 𝐶 𝑟 𝑖 and 𝐶 𝑤 𝑖 to be constant. Accordingly, the worst case timing value for the execution phase is determined using the equation, 𝐶 𝑒 𝑚𝑎𝑥 𝑖 = (1 -𝛾) • 𝐶 𝑖 . The best case timing for the execution phase is determined using the relationship,
div.formula: 𝐶 𝑒 𝑚𝑖𝑛 𝑖 = 𝛽 • 𝐶 𝑒 𝑚𝑎𝑥

div.head: 𝑖
div.p: . If execution is contention-free, the variability of execution time on multi-core platforms is significantly reduced [15]. Thus, we set 𝛽 = 0.9 in all our experiments. Furthermore, in all our experiments we consider 𝑇 𝑖 = 𝐷 𝑖 and 𝑂 𝑖 = 0. The priorities, 𝑃 𝑖 are assigned according to the rate monotonic order. Additionally, all of these task parameters were scaled to fit the 16bit integer precision used in UPPAAL. In all of our experiments, a timeout of 1 hour is set. If the UPPAAL model does not provide a schedulability result within this timeout, we consider that task set to be unschedulable. The percentage of occurred timeouts is also plotted for each experiment (ET Timeout in Figure 3). If not otherwise stated, 200 generated task sets are used for each plotted data point.

div.head: Schedulability evaluation
div.p: Four different types of experiments are performed to evaluate the proposed test and to compare it with the SOTA from a perspective of schedulability ratio. We use a basic configuration of, 𝑈 = 1, 𝑚 = 4,𝛾 = 0.1 and 𝑛 = 10 and vary one of these values in each experiment.

div.head: Varying Utilization.
div.p: The first experiment evaluates the schedulability of task sets by varying their total utilization. 𝑈 is varied from 0.1 to 2.0 in increments of 0.1 (see Figure 3a). The percentage of schedulable tasksets decrease with the increase of 𝑈 in both the proposed test and the SOTA. No timeouts are observed for any of the utilization values. The proposed test provides more schedulable task sets than the SOTA for all the 𝑈 values, with a maximum difference at 𝑈 = 0.5, where 65% more schedulable task sets are observed compared to the SOTA.

div.head: Varying number of Cores.
div.p: The second experiment evaluates the schedulability of task sets by varying the number of cores (𝑚) from 1 to 7 (see Figure 3b). For both tests, the percentage of schedulable task sets starts to saturate at 𝑚 = 5. This shows that having more cores does not help after some point when the memory access resource is limited. The proposed test can classify up to 64% more task sets as schedulable than SOTA (at 𝑚 = 6). No timeout is observed for all values of 𝑚.

div.head: Varying Memory Ratio per
div.p: Task. The third experiment evaluates the schedulability of the task sets with a varying memory to execution phase ratio (see Figure 3c). The memory ratio (𝛾 = 𝐶 𝑤 𝑖 +𝐶 𝑟 𝑖 𝐶 𝑖 ) per task is varied from 0.1 to 1.0 in increments of 0.1. The percentage of schedulable task sets decreases with the increase of 𝛾 as expected. The reason is, memory access being the limitation and bottleneck in multi-core systems (see Sec.6.1.2). Thus, larger memory phases increase the difficulty of the scheduling problem of the memory phases. No timeouts are observed in this experiment as well.

div.head: Varying number of
div.p: Tasks per Task Set. The fourth experiment evaluates the schedulability of task sets by varying the number of tasks per task set from 2 to 20 (see Figure 3d). The schedulable percentage of task sets decreases with the increase of 𝑛 as expected. It is interesting to notice that the timeouts start to increase around 𝑛 = 15. Meaning that, UPPAAL is unable to find a solution for some task sets before the timeout. The reachability problem gets complex as the state space increases with 𝑛. We used 𝑛 = 10 for the rest of the experiments above as it gives a large enough system to provide interesting results as well as give solutions fast enough.

div.head: Runtime evaluation
div.p: The solving time is the time taken for UPPAAL to determine a task set as schedulable or unschedulable. The solving time depends on the complexity of the state space of the reachability problem. The more possible scheduling scenarios present, the more solving time needed. Figure 3e shows the solving times for the experiment with a varying number of tasks (see Sec. 6.1.4). A box plot is used, where the median time for each 𝑛 value is represented by a red horizontal strip. A box represents the interquartile range. A cross represents an outlier. When 𝑛 increases the number of jobs that need to be scheduled within a hyperperiod increases. With this, the state space increases as well and the solving time grows exponentially. We can conclude that in our setting, up to 𝑛 = 15 our test returns a solution fairly fast. The median solving time is below 1s up to 12 tasks and the average solving time is below 1s up to 8 tasks.

div.head: log-uniform period distribution
div.p: All of our experiments show the pessimism in the SOTA test. In this experiment, we evaluate the effect of a log-uniform period distribution on the performance of the proposed test (Figure 3f). We use period values with log-uniform distribution between 10 and 100ms while varying the total utilization 𝑈 . Each plotted point represents 100 task sets. For low and medium utilization values, the SOTA method has a higher schedulability percentage, while the proposed test experiences increased timeouts. The reason for a bigger number of timeouts is large hyperperiods that in turn lead to a large number of jobs that need to be scheduled within a hyperperiod. The largest observed hyperperiod in the experiment is 2450701344 ms (about 28 days), and the largest number of jobs in one hyperperiod is 166297739. Therefore, the scalability of our test depends greatly on the number of jobs that need to be scheduled within one hyperperiod.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Contention when accessing shared resources poses several challenges for real-time applications on multi-core platforms. The AER model circumvents this problem by allowing only one task to access shared resources at a time. Thus, contention is avoided by design. This work presents an exact schedulability test for the AER model under global fixed-priority scheduling. Being an exact test, it provides a baseline against which other tests can be compared. We first discuss how the problem can be modelled as self-suspending tasks, where we highlight details that warrant a dedicated schedulability test. The proposed schedulability test uses timed automata, where the schedulability problem is mapped to a reachability problem. Our results show that the proposed test can find up to 65% more schedulable task sets for the evaluated cases than the state-of-the-art while solving times remain in an acceptable range.
